overview: The atlas paints “Sasanian dependencies” across Yemen from 600 to 800, but the real story is a lightning-fast imperial arrival followed by two centuries of change. Persian troops under Vahrez crossed the sea around 570, defeated an Aksumite-backed ruler, installed a tributary king and later kept governors and soldiers near Sana'a. Those settlers formed families with local women; their descendants were called Abna. When the Sasanian state collapsed after 628, Badhan and other leaders accepted Islam, and Yemen entered the world of the first caliphs. The Persian dynasty itself ended in 651. This card therefore treats the 700 layer as an atlas afterimage. It follows Yemen's older dams, farms, scripts and faiths; Persian strategy and mixed families; plague, trade, clothes, music and water; then Umayyad and Abbasid successors. The polygon stays still, but history races underneath it.

periods.title: Aksumite conquest and Abraha's Yemen
periods.summary: Aksum intervened in 525 after a deadly religious conflict. Abraha later ruled from Yemen, repaired Marib's dam and recorded Christian kingship in local Sabaic as well as an Ethiopian imperial setting.

periods.title: Persian ships, Vahrez and a tributary king
periods.summary: Khosrow I sent Vahrez and a small expedition. They defeated Masruq, installed Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan as a tributary, then returned after Sayf's death and left troops and governors around Sana'a.

periods.title: A distant Sasanian garrison in a Yemeni landscape
periods.summary: Persian governors and soldiers formed one ruling group among Yemeni nobles, tribes, farmers, traders and religious communities. The atlas begins here, but its giant label hides negotiated and uneven authority.

periods.title: Imperial collapse and a local change of allegiance
periods.summary: After Byzantine victories and crisis in Iraq isolated the garrison, governor Badhan and Abna leaders accepted Islam. Uprisings and fighting followed; Persian-descended families did not simply vanish with the old command chain.

periods.title: Yemen under the first caliphs while Iran falls
periods.summary: Medinan armies and Yemeni allies secured the region as Muslim forces defeated Sasanian armies, took Ctesiphon and ended Yazdegerd III's dynasty in 651. Yemen was already outside Sasanian rule.

periods.title: Umayyad provinces, not a Persian dependency
periods.summary: Under Muawiya, Yemen was divided into a northern region centered on Sana'a and a southern one centered on al-Janad. Local ties and difficult terrain still mattered inside caliphal administration.

periods.title: Abbasid Yemen and an atlas afterimage
periods.summary: Abbasid authority linked Yemen to wider Red Sea and Indian Ocean worlds, but distance limited control. The atlas keeps the old dependency polygon until 800, then finally hands it to an Abbasid layer.

sections.title: Read the painted label before the history

items.text: The exact atlas id is sasanian-dependencies, displayed as “Sasanian dependencies.” It is a circa state covering 600 to 800 and has no aliases, summary or linked historical article in the index. That plural label invites caution: it describes an editorial map category, not the name of a single dynasty or Yemeni kingdom.

In 500 the target does not exist. The atlas puts Najran, Sana'a, Marib and Shibam/Hadramawt inside himyarite-kingdom, while Ctesiphon, Istakhr, Gundeshapur and other Iranian or Iraqi tests belong to a separate sasanian-empire feature. The later dependency card therefore concerns Yemen, not the Persian imperial heartland.

In 600 the target is one Polygon, one ring and 57 positions, with a bounding box from about 41.20° to 52.36° east and 12.61° to 19.18° north. Najran, Sana'a, Marib and Shibam/Hadramawt test inside; Aden, Socotra, Mecca, Oman, Iraq and Iran test outside.

The 700 target is byte-for-byte the same 57-position polygon with the same bounding box and SHA-256. The atlas also continues a separate sasanian-empire shape over much of Iran. Both are historical afterimages: Yemen changed allegiance around 631 to 632, and the Sasanian dynasty ended in 651, long before this layer closes.

At 800 the dependency id vanishes. The atlas assigns tested Najran, Sana'a, Marib and Shibam/Hadramawt to abbasid-caliphate, and does the same for tested Ctesiphon, Istakhr and Gundeshapur. This is an editorial handoff, not a conquest in exactly 800; the real political transitions happened in several earlier stages.

Aksumite forces crossed from northeast Africa in 525 during a conflict in which a Jewish Himyarite king had attacked Christians. Their inscriptions presented conquest through Christian language and Ethiopian identity. That matters because Persian intervention around 570 displaced an Aksumite-backed order; it did not arrive in an empty or religiously uniform land.

Late pre-Islamic Yemen included Jewish and Christian communities alongside older South Arabian traditions. The Persian colony's own religious path is surprisingly unclear: the best account says we do not know whether it retained Zoroastrian practice, joined local Christianity or otherwise assimilated. A Sasanian flag cannot serve as a faith census.

Marib's dam and canals created an enormous artificial oasis in a dry landscape. Cities, temples, walls and inscriptions reveal centuries of local organization and engineering extending to Islam's arrival around 630. Persian governors inherited this achievement; describing every canal as “Sasanian technology” would erase the Yemeni builders who made and maintained it.

An inscription records the Great Dam's rupture in 547, an outbreak of plague that halted repair, and work resuming when the outbreak eased. Tribes completed major stone construction before Abraha returned to Sana'a in 548. It is rare, vivid evidence for labor, disease and public works just before the Persian conquest.

A short line from CIH 541, carved at Marib in March 548, reads 𐩨𐩭𐩺𐩡 𐩥[𐩧]𐩵𐩱 𐩥𐩧𐩢𐩣𐩩 𐩧𐩢𐩣𐩬𐩬. Editorial transliteration: “b-ḫyl w-[r]dʾ w-rḥmt rḥmnn”; translation: “By the power and [a]id and mercy of Raḥmānān.” It is a normalized Old South Arabian script rendering, not a facsimile, and directly represents Yemen's Christian Sabaic tradition immediately before Persian rule.

sections.title: Why Khosrow sent Vahrez so far

items.text: A Yemeni prince, Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, sought outside help against Masruq's Ethiopian-backed regime. Khosrow I eventually sent Vahrez with a small force by sea. After victory, Sayf ruled as Persia's tributary vassal. The arrangement began as client kingship, not an instant Persian province with identical rules everywhere.

When Sayf was killed after only a few years, Vahrez returned with a larger force. Persian soldiers and officials then remained near Sana'a under successive governors. This second intervention explains why the atlas has a dependency at all, but the record still names local rulers, allies and resistance rather than total control from village to village.

Yemen stood beside routes joining India, the Red Sea, northeast Africa and the Mediterranean. Persian and Ethiopian competition therefore involved shipping, customs, prestige and access as well as religion. Ships carrying valuable goods make a better explanation for distant imperial interest than the idea that Khosrow simply liked collecting faraway colors on a map.

Across Arabia, Sasanian rulers mixed methods: direct garrisons in some strategic places, treaties or tributary rulers in others, and tribal alliances that could change. Yemen's Persian force fits that wider pattern. “Dependency” is therefore a useful atlas shorthand only if readers remember that negotiated influence and military settlement were not the same thing.

The Lakhmid kings at Hira guarded desert approaches, negotiated with Arab groups and fought for Sasanian interests. Khosrow II abolished their dynasty before the final crisis, weakening one long-used client system. Their story helps explain the term dependency, but Hira is outside this card's Yemen polygon and must not be folded into its geography.

sections.title: Power, war and the limits of a distant empire

items.text: The Sasanian state in Iran could mobilize courts, armies, taxation, priestly institutions, coinage and long traditions of kingship. Its rulers fought Rome and Byzantium on an enormous scale. Yemen's garrison drew prestige from that empire, yet a few governors at Sana'a were never a miniature copy of Ctesiphon's whole government.

A dependency could send tribute, host troops or follow an imperial ally without every local decision traveling to Persia. Archaeology across Arabia is uneven, so written stories can make imperial reach look cleaner than it was. The card separates documented garrisons and governors from unprovable claims about continuous control of the entire painted polygon.

The Persian settlement changed through contact. One governor's son, Khurra Khosrow, was reportedly so arabized that the king replaced him. The same source records mountain unrest over Persian financial demands. Those clues show adaptation and resistance together: becoming locally connected did not make taxes cheerful or imperial orders easy.

Persian strategy around the southern seas also aimed to protect shipping and collect customs. Ports and overland communities did not all depend on the same road, season or political bargain. Trade made Yemen valuable, while Yemen's mountains and local leaders made it hard to command, a combination empires often discover the expensive way.

Sasanian law in the imperial core classified people by freedom, citizenship, religion, social rank, gender and age. That reveals a sharply unequal world, but no checked source proves the same courts applied every rule identically in Yemen. It is safer to say the garrison carried status ideas than to invent a province-wide legal code.

Persian soldiers and officials settled around Sana'a and married local Arab women. Their children and descendants were called Abna, “sons.” This is the clearest family evidence for the dependency: homes and kinship turned a foreign garrison into a locally rooted community whose members remained visible during the first Islamic century.

In Sasanian Iran, a free adult noble Zoroastrian man held legal advantages that women, children, enslaved people, foreigners and religious minorities did not share. Yemen had its own norms and rulers, so this is imperial background rather than a household census. Either way, power was distributed very unequally by birth and status.

A much earlier Marib decree regulated sales, loans and the enslavement of people. Its third-century date means it cannot be quoted as law in 600, but it proves that written rules and slavery belonged to the region's inherited social history. Hard truth: some households' comfort depended on other people's constrained labor.

Early Islamic political organization reshaped what “Yemeni” meant, and later writers remembered little of the old polyglot, terraced and incense-trading past. Families did not wake up in 632 with one new identity. Tribal connection, town, faith, language, Persian ancestry and loyalty could overlap or change across generations.

Wahb ibn Munabbih came from a Yemeni family with Persian connections and became a major early transmitter of historical and religious lore. His career shows learning inside a mixed post-conquest society. It also warns us that stories preserved later are interpretation, not a video recording of his grandparents' daily life.

Yemen's position linked Indian Ocean cargoes with Red Sea and overland routes. Sailors, port workers, camel drivers, guards, brokers and tax collectors all helped goods move, though the sources spotlight rulers more than laborers. Commerce did not erase risk: changing alliances, storms and demands for customs could interrupt a profitable journey.

The Marib system diverted seasonal water through canals to cultivate a vast oasis. Farmers and water managers had to clear, repair and negotiate access to this inherited infrastructure. The achievement belongs to centuries of South Arabian practice, not one governor. A polygon can change color faster than a field learns to drink.

A Shabwa incense burner pictures a camel rider, while the museum record explains the animal's value for transport, milk and hair as well as meat. The object is third-century, so it supplies earlier regional context rather than a 600 menu. Camels carried economies; they were not merely scenery behind battles.

Shabwa also earned income from salt and sat on routes toward Najran and the coast. Salt, animals, cultivated produce and imported goods could meet in markets, yet no checked source gives an average family's shopping list for 600 to 800. Food likely varied sharply by altitude, season, wealth and access to irrigation.

After the conquest, Yemen remained part of a Red Sea zone of economic and social interaction rather than becoming isolated. Connections ran toward the Hejaz and northeast Africa while wider caliphal trade patterns changed. Political rulers changed more quickly than sailors' knowledge of winds, ports and trustworthy partners.

sections.title: Homes, clothes, crafts and a little music

items.text: At earlier Shabwa, crowded tower houses had thick rectangular stone foundations with upper parts of wood and unfired mudbrick; inscriptions even mention several storeys. This is excellent regional building evidence but predates the card. It helps explain why masonry survives while roofs, mats and ordinary upstairs belongings often disappear.

Dhafar's landscape preserves rock-cut and built structures beside farms, dams and cisterns. Households depended on careful use of seasonal rain in a highland environment without perennial water. The surviving monumental features reveal setting and skill, while most bedding, baskets, toys and everyday wooden tools left a much fainter trace.

An eighth to ninth-century shawl attributed to Sana'a is cotton embroidered with wool. Its survival shows skilled textile work during the Umayyad-Abbasid successor period, just after this atlas interval. It cannot dress every earlier resident for us, but it proves that cloth production remained a celebrated Yemeni craft.

A tiny first to second-century bronze shows a seated woman playing a lyre. Museum curators stress that evidence for pre-Islamic Yemeni music is fragmentary, although lyres, lutes and drums appear in images and later reports. It suggests performance at feasts or ceremonies, not mandatory lyre lessons for every child in 650.

Excavation and mapping at Zafar keep finding important sixth-century material, but erosion, later building and destruction have removed context. That makes ordinary play especially hard to recover. Children surely did more than watch adults work, yet the checked archaeology does not supply a securely dated toy box or game rulebook.

sections.title: Faith, languages and who could learn

items.text: Zoroastrian institutions were closely linked to Sasanian kingship in Iran, while Christians, Jews, Manichaeans and others also lived across the empire. Yemen's religious history followed its own path. A Persian officer may have known Zoroastrian practice, but the colony's actual beliefs are too poorly documented to label every Abna household.

The Marib invocation uses Sabaic in Ancient South Arabian script for Christian language, while Aksumite conquerors also erected Ge'ez inscriptions. Scripts and languages carried political identity. By the seventh century Arabic grew more important, but an alphabet change was gradual and did not make everybody literate overnight.

Later Muslim-era communities often could not read the old South Arabian inscriptions around them, and early Arabic literature preserved only fragments of the polyglot past. That is a useful lesson about education: knowledge can be lost even when stones survive. No checked source gives a universal school system for dependency-era children.

Wahb ibn Munabbih and other Abna-associated scholars became known for religious traditions and stories in the early Islamic period. Learning could travel through families, teachers and scholarly circles. Their visibility cannot be turned into a literacy rate: farmers' children, servants and elite sons did not receive equal time, books or instruction.

The Sana'a shawl carries an Arabic inscription translated by the museum as “In the name of God. Blessing from God. Of what was made in the tiraz of Sana'a.” It dates to the eighth to ninth century and identifies a textile workshop, so it is successor-era evidence for writing woven into work, faith and prestige.

sections.title: Illness, water, and the missing toilet

items.text: The 547 plague outbreak stopped work at Marib's dam; leaders dismissed assembled tribes, and repairs resumed after the outbreak eased. The inscription records disruption and timing, not symptoms or a cure. It proves that epidemic disease could reorganize labor while leaving us almost nothing about bedside care for an ordinary child.

Gondeshapur in Khuzestan became famous for medical learning and later transmission of Galenic traditions. It belonged to the Sasanian imperial core, not this Yemen polygon, and scholars debate the exact shape of its early hospital. It would be exciting, but false, to place a Gondeshapur clinic in every town the atlas colors.

At Dhafar, open reservoirs served irrigation and animals, while enclosed cisterns stored drinking water. This distinction shows practical attention to water quality in a seasonal-rain landscape. It does not prove germ theory or pipes in every house; carrying, storing and rationing water remained household work with unequal burdens.

Archaeologists at Zafar recover strong walls more readily than timber, wattle, daub or small household fittings. In the sources checked, no securely dated Sasanian or early Islamic Yemeni household latrine has been identified. That is an evidence statement, not proof that people had no private ways to manage waste.

Marib's sluices and Dhafar's cisterns managed precious water, but neither is automatically a sewer. Water engineering deserves admiration without turning every channel into plumbing. Put less politely: a dam has an outlet, not a giant toilet seat. The joke follows the archaeology, the sanitation hardware itself remains undocumented here.

sections.title: Conquest, successor states and what continued

items.text: By 628 Byzantine victories and civil crisis left Persian agents across Arabia without reliable support. Badhan and leading Abna accepted Islam around 631. That local switch came before Muslim armies conquered the Sasanian heartland, so Yemen's dependency ended through isolation and changed allegiance rather than one battle at Sana'a in 651.

The years around 632 were violent. Rival Yemeni leaders challenged Badhan's successors and targeted Abna families; Firuz and allies resisted, and a force sent by Abu Bakr helped restore Muslim authority. Persian-descended residents survived as neighbors, soldiers and scholars even though their imperial chain of command did not.

In Iran, Muslim forces won at Qadisiyya in 636, took Ctesiphon in 637 and defeated another major army at Nihavand in 642. Yazdegerd III was killed in 651, ending the dynasty. Those dates make the atlas problem unmistakable: a Sasanian dependency cannot remain politically Sasanian through 800.

Under the Umayyads, Yemen was divided between a northern region centered on Sana'a and a southern one around al-Janad. Abbasid rulers after 750 found the region difficult to control because of distance and tribal politics. These are successor administrations inside the atlas's unchanged old polygon, not a revived Persian dependency.

A silver drachm minted at Yazd in 662 still shows Khosrow II's bust and a fire altar under Arab-Sasanian authority. The coin comes from Iran, not Yemen, but it offers a perfect continuity lesson: governments can fall while money designs, officials and habits continue. Political ending is not cultural amnesia.

ending.text: The 800 endpoint is an atlas handoff to abbasid-caliphate, not the fall of a still-living Sasanian dependency. Persian rule in Yemen had changed into Muslim allegiance around 631 to 632, and Yazdegerd III's dynasty ended in 651. Abna families, administrative habits and Persian cultural forms continued, while Yemen's local farming, trade and social networks adapted under Umayyad and Abbasid power.
